Summary:\n\n## Now uses a single ssh identity (root) for everything peer-related\n\n- `deploy_to_peer` ssh's as root (binary tarball + extraction)\n- `peer_already_has_version` ssh's as root (.built-version check)\n- `provision_peer` ssh's as root (serve.sh + /etc/init.d/ollama + service ops)\n\n## Why this fixes your error\n\nYour error was `Permission denied` when scp'ing `serve.sh` into `/home/sora/programs/ollama/` as the `sora` user. Root ssh writes through unmolested.\n\n## One-time peer prep (per peer, before this script runs from the build host)\n\nOn each peer, as root, once:\n\n```\nsed -i 's/^#*PermitRootLogin.*/PermitRootLogin prohibit-password/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config\nrc-service sshd restart\n```\n\nThen from the build host:\n\n```\nssh-keygen -t ed25519\nssh-copy-id root@192.168.1.11\nssh-copy-id root@192.168.1.12\nssh-copy-id root@192.168.1.13\n```\n\n(The `ssh-copy-id` to the build host's own IP isn't strictly needed since we don't ssh to ourselves — but it won't hurt and keeps the three hosts symmetric.)\n\n## What re-running will do\n\nYou're on sora2 (192.168.1.12). The script will:\n\n1. Skip the build (cached, version matches).\n2. Package the binary.\n3. Skip deploy to sora1 and sora3 (peer_already_has_version reports match).\n4. Provision sora1 and sora3 (write serve.sh, install openrc unit, start service).\n5. Provision sora2 locally (write serve.sh, install openrc unit, start service).\n\nAfter that, you should be able to curl each of:\n\n```\ncurl http://192.168.1.11:10101/api/tags\ncurl http://192.168.1.12:20202/api/tags\ncurl http://192.168.1.13:30303/api/tags\n```\n\nUntil the ssh keys are copied, you'll still see password prompts for root@peer — type the password each time, or stop, set up keys, and re-run."

        "text":"That's the chicken-and-egg of `PermitRootLogin prohibit-password`: it blocks password auth for root, so `ssh-copy-id` (which uses password auth to push the key) can't push the very first key. There are two ways out.\n\n## Option A (recommended): paste the key manually\n\nYou already have root shells on all three hosts. Just bypass ssh-copy-id and place the key directly.\n\n**On sora1**, display the public key:\n\n```\ncat /root/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub\n```\n\nIt'll be one line: `ssh-ed25519 AAAA... root@fg-sora-1`. Copy it.\n\n**On sora2 and sora3** (you're already root on each):\n\n```\nmkdir -p /root/.ssh\nchmod 700 /root/.ssh\necho 'ssh-ed25519 AAAA...whatever you copied... root@fg-sora-1' >> /root/.ssh/authorized_keys\nchmod 600 /root/.ssh/authorized_keys\n```\n\nThen test from sora1:\n\n```\nssh root@192.168.1.12 whoami\nssh root@192.168.1.13 whoami\n```\n\nShould print `root` with no password prompt.\n\n## Option B: temporarily relax sshd, then revert\n\nIf you'd rather use ssh-copy-id: on each peer, flip back to `yes`, copy the key, flip back to `prohibit-password`:\n\n```\nsed -i 's/PermitRootLogin prohibit-password/PermitRootLogin yes/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config\nrc-service sshd reload\n# (now ssh-copy-id from sora1 works)\nsed -i 's/PermitRootLogin yes/PermitRootLogin prohibit-password/' /etc/ssh/sshd_config\nrc-service sshd reload\n```\n\nMore steps; same end state.\n\n## One thing to verify on your key\n\nThe `ssh-keygen` prompted you for a passphrase. **If you set one**, every ssh from the script will hang waiting for it. For an automation key that only sits inside this private LAN, an empty passphrase is the right call. Check with:\n\n```\nssh-keygen -y -f /root/.ssh/id_ed25519 < /dev/null\n```\n\nIf it prints the public key with no prompt, you have no passphrase (good). If it prompts for one, regenerate with `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N ''` and replace the authorized_keys entries on sora2/sora3 with the new pubkey."
      }]

    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"Easy fix — strip the passphrase from the existing key without regenerating. That preserves the public key, so the `authorized_keys` entries on sora2 and sora3 stay valid.\n\n```\nssh-keygen -p -f /root/.ssh/id_ed25519\n```\n\nEnter your current passphrase when prompted, then hit Enter twice for an empty new passphrase. Verify:\n\n```\nssh root@192.168.1.12 whoami\n```\n\nShould print `root` instantly with no prompt at all.\n\n## If you'd rather keep the passphrase\n\nYou'd need `ssh-agent` running and the key added (`ssh-add /root/.ssh/id_ed25519`) once per shell session before invoking the script. The script itself won't prompt because ssh will pull the unlocked key from the agent. More secure (passphrase never on disk in cleartext), more friction (manual `ssh-add` before each session).\n\nFor a service-account key on a private LAN that's only used by a build script, stripping the passphrase is the conventional call — and it's what most automation setups do."
      }]
  },

        "type":"text",
        "text":"It's a cosmetic warning from busybox, not an error. ssh-copy-id is a shell script that internally uses `expr` to grep for error strings, and busybox's `expr` is stricter than GNU's about regex portability — it warns when a pattern starts with `^` (treating \"^\" as an anchor is GNU's behavior; strict POSIX BRE treats the first character literally, and busybox flags the divergence).\n\nNothing's broken. ssh-copy-id worked fine — the \"All keys were skipped because they already exist\" message confirms the key is already installed from your earlier ssh-copy-id runs. Your two `whoami` calls returned `root` with no prompt, which is the actual proof the auth chain is working end-to-end.\n\nYou can ignore the warning. It'll appear every time ssh-copy-id runs on busybox; it's an Alpine + ssh-copy-id quirk that has nothing to do with the keys themselves.\n\nReady to re-run `./ollama-build-and-deploy.sh` — should sail through with no prompts now."
      }]
  },

        "type":"text",
        "text":"Two things to address:\n\n## 1. Log fix (script updated)\n\nSwitched the OpenRC unit to log to `/var/log/ollama/ollama.log` and added a `start_pre()` block that uses OpenRC's `checkpath` to create the directory with `sora:sora` ownership before the daemon starts. Idempotent and runs on every service start, so it survives reboots and tmpfs clears.\n\nRe-copy the script to sora1, then re-run there. The `[ ok ]` was misleading — Ollama may have started anyway with stdout going nowhere. You can confirm whether the current service is actually live with:\n\n```\ncurl http://192.168.1.11:10101/api/tags\n```\n\nIf you get JSON back, it was running despite the log error. If you get connection refused, the daemon never came up.\n\n## 2. The mesh-ssh decision\n\nYou're running on each of the three hosts in turn. That means each host needs to ssh as root to the other two — currently only sora1 → {sora2, sora3} works (you set those keys up). Sora2 and sora3 hit the password prompt because their keys aren't on sora1.\n\nThree options, in order of effort:\n\n**a. Designate sora1 as the build host.** Don't run the script on sora2/sora3 ever again — just from sora1. Zero more ssh setup needed.\n\n**b. Share one keypair across all three hosts.** From sora1, push its own keypair to the other two so all three present the same identity:\n\n```\nscp /root/.ssh/id_ed25519 /root/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub root@192.168.1.12:/root/.ssh/\nscp /root/.ssh/id_ed25519 /root/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub root@192.168.1.13:/root/.ssh/\nssh root@192.168.1.12 'cat /root/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub >> /root/.ssh/authorized_keys'\nssh root@192.168.1.13 'cat /root/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub >> /root/.ssh/authorized_keys'\ncat /root/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub >> /root/.ssh/authorized_keys\n```\n\nAfter that, any of the three hosts can ssh to any other as root. Six ssh-directions, one shared key. Pragmatic for a closed cluster.\n\n**c. Per-host keys with mesh authorization.** Generate a separate keypair on sora2 and sora3, then `ssh-copy-id` each to the other two. More conventional from a security separation standpoint; more setup steps.\n\nIf you don't have a reason to keep separate identities, (b) is the shortest road to \"I can run this script from any host.\" (a) is the road of least resistance if you don't mind always working from sora1.\n\nWhich do you want?"
      }]

        "type":"text",
        "text":"Local daemon on sora1 is up. Sora2 and sora3 say \"started\" but aren't accepting connections — that means the daemon process forked, then probably crashed immediately. OpenRC's `[ ok ]` only confirms the fork, not that the daemon stayed alive.\n\nOne-shot diagnostic on each peer:\n\n```\nssh root@192.168.1.12 'rc-service ollama status; echo \"---log---\"; cat /tmp/ollama/ollama.log; echo \"---serve.sh---\"; cat /home/sora/programs/ollama/serve.sh; echo \"---listen---\"; ss -tlnp | grep -E \"10101|20202|30303\" || echo \"(nothing listening)\"'\n```\n\nAnd the same for `.13`. Paste the output. The likely culprits:\n\n- **Bind IP not on the interface.** If sora2's actual interface IP differs from `192.168.1.12`, the daemon will fail to bind. The serve.sh dump shows what it's trying to bind.\n- **Daemon crashed for some other reason.** The log will show why — could be a port conflict, an OOM, a missing model directory permission, anything.\n- **Process started but bound to `127.0.0.1`.** If something in the env is overriding `OLLAMA_HOST`, the daemon will only listen locally even though serve.sh exports the right address.\n\nThe `ss -tlnp` line at the end tells us what (if anything) is actually listening — that's the ground truth, regardless of what OpenRC reports."
      }]
  },

        "text":"That long command got mangled by terminal wrap — the single-quoted argument got split across lines, the shell closed the quote at the wrong spot, and half of it ran locally on whichever host that shell is on (looks like sora3 based on the serve.sh dump that ended up local). Also `ss` isn't in busybox; we want `netstat`.\n\nLet me give it to you as separate one-shot commands so quoting can't break. Run these from any shell where root ssh to .12 works:\n\n```\nssh root@192.168.1.12 cat /home/sora/programs/ollama/serve.sh\n```\n```\nssh root@192.168.1.12 rc-service ollama status\n```\n```\nssh root@192.168.1.12 cat /tmp/ollama/ollama.log\n```\n```\nssh root@192.168.1.12 netstat -tln\n```\n\nThen the same four for `.13`:\n\n```\nssh root@192.168.1.13 cat /home/sora/programs/ollama/serve.sh\nssh root@192.168.1.13 rc-service ollama status\nssh root@192.168.1.13 cat /tmp/ollama/ollama.log\nssh root@192.168.1.13 netstat -tln\n```\n\nPaste each block's output. The four things I'm watching for:\n\n- **`serve.sh`**: does it have the correct `BIND_IP` and `PORT` for that host (`.12`/`20202` and `.13`/`30303`)? If sora1 ran provision correctly, yes; if not, that's the bug.\n- **`rc-service status`**: `started` vs `stopped`. If stopped, the daemon crashed and OpenRC noticed.\n- **`/tmp/ollama/ollama.log`**: the actual stdout/stderr from the daemon. If it crashed, the reason is here.\n- **`netstat -tln`**: what's actually listening. If 20202/30303 don't appear, the daemon never bound.\n\nOne side note about the earlier output — the serve.sh you saw with `BIND_IP=\"192.168.1.13\"` was almost certainly your *current shell's local* serve.sh (because the broken ssh quoting made the `cat` run locally), not sora2's. So we don't actually have any signal yet about what's on sora2 or sora3."
      }]

        "type":"text",
        "text":"Found it. The log shows the smoking gun:\n\n```\n/bin/sh: can't open '/home/sora/programs/ollama/serve.sh': Permission denied\n```\n\n`serve.sh` on sora2 has the right contents, but its mode is too restrictive — sora can't read it. The chain of events:\n\n1. We `scp`'d the file as root. The sshd-side sftp subsystem creates new files using its own umask, which on Alpine often ends up restrictive (mode `600` — only root can read).\n2. Our remote `chmod +x` just adds the execute bit on existing permissions. So `600` becomes `700`. Still root-only.\n3. When OpenRC tries to start the service as `sora`, `sora` can't open the file.\n\n`chmod +x` was the wrong primitive. We need explicit `chmod 755` on the remote so the file ends up readable + executable by everyone:"
      }]
  },

        "text":"Why sora1 worked despite the bug: in `provision_local`, the file is created by `>` redirect with the local shell's umask (typically `0022` when run by root via interactive shell), so the file starts at `644`. `chmod +x` lifts that to `755`. World-readable. But scp's destination mode is set by sshd's umask, which is often `0077` (giving `600` initial) — and `chmod +x` then only gets to `700`.\n\nNow both paths use explicit `chmod 755` so the result is the same regardless of umask.\n\n## Re-copy and re-run\n\n```\nscp /tmp/ollama-build-and-deploy.sh root@192.168.1.11:/home/sora/programs/ollama/ollama-build-and-deploy.sh\nssh root@192.168.1.11 /home/sora/programs/ollama/ollama-build-and-deploy.sh\n```\n\n(Adjust the first scp to wherever you've been editing the script.)\n\nAfter it finishes, the three curls should all return JSON:\n\n```\ncurl http://192.168.1.11:10101/api/tags\ncurl http://192.168.1.12:20202/api/tags\ncurl http://192.168.1.13:30303/api/tags\n```\n\nOnce that works, you're ready to `ollama pull qwen2.5:3b`."
      }]
  },

        "text":"All three endpoints up and answering. Just one more layer of plumbing — the CLI defaults to `127.0.0.1:11434`, but our daemons are bound to specific IPs on non-default ports, so you have to point the client at the right address.\n\nTo pull `qwen2.5:3b` on sora1:\n\n```\nOLLAMA_HOST=192.168.1.11:10101 /home/sora/programs/ollama/bin/ollama pull qwen2.5:3b\n```\n\nThat'll pull ~2 GB and store it in `/home/sora/programs/ollama/models/` on sora1 (where that daemon's `OLLAMA_MODELS` points). Once it's done, verify:\n\n```\ncurl http://192.168.1.11:10101/api/tags\n```\n\nYou should see the model listed instead of an empty array.\n\nFor the other two hosts, you'd pull separately (each daemon stores models in its own host's `/home/sora/programs/ollama/models/` — they don't share storage):\n\n```\nOLLAMA_HOST=192.168.1.12:20202 /home/sora/programs/ollama/bin/ollama pull qwen2.5:3b\nOLLAMA_HOST=192.168.1.13:30303 /home/sora/programs/ollama/bin/ollama pull qwen2.5:3b\n```\n\nOr, faster, pull once on sora1 and rsync the result to the other two:\n\n```\nssh root@192.168.1.12 'rm -rf /home/sora/programs/ollama/models && mkdir -p /home/sora/programs/ollama/models'\nrsync -a /home/sora/programs/ollama/models/ root@192.168.1.12:/home/sora/programs/ollama/models/\nssh root@192.168.1.12 chown -R sora:sora /home/sora/programs/ollama/models\nssh root@192.168.1.12 rc-service ollama restart\n```\n\nEither path works.\n\n## A small QoL tip\n\nIf you'll be running `ollama` a lot, drop these in `/root/.profile` (or wherever your shell reads) on each host so the CLI just works:\n\n```\nexport PATH=\"/home/sora/programs/ollama/bin:$PATH\"\nexport OLLAMA_HOST=\"192.168.1.11:10101\"   # use this host's own IP:port\n```\n\nThen `ollama pull qwen2.5:3b` from a shell on sora1 talks directly to sora1's daemon.\n\nOnce the model is pulled, smoke test:\n\n```\nOLLAMA_HOST=192.168.1.11:10101 /home/sora/programs/ollama/bin/ollama run qwen2.5:3b \"What is 17 squared?\"\n```\n\nIf you get `289` back in a sentence, the entire stack — bootstrap, build, deploy, runtime, model — is end-to-end working."
